run_id.description: Identity of this routing observation. `decision_id` is a hash of the task, so repeated runs of one task share it; `run_id` keeps those runs distinguishable from duplicated records. It does not identify the enclosing execution and must never be redefined to — see `execution_run_id`.

execution_run_id.description: Identifier of the enclosing execution outcome when this routing observation occurred within an execution. Absent for standalone routing observations such as CLI shadow runs. Historical pre-correlation observations remain valid without it: absence means correlation was not recorded, not that the observation is invalid, and they are not backfilled. Distinct from `run_id`, which identifies this observation rather than the run around it.

selected_route.description: Which execution strategy carried this routing decision. It identifies the strategy, never the concrete model: `local-shadow` is local model inference, `deterministic-local` is local execution with no model inference at all, `cloud-required` means the policy requires cloud execution, and `approved-local` is a reserved promotion state that is not a legitimate runtime write. Model identity stays in `local_model`, which is null when the strategy runs no model. Values like `qwen-local` or `gpt-cloud` would collapse the two and are therefore not admissible here.

application.description: Whether this routing decision affected a real execution. `advisory` is a recommendation only, with no model call and no run affected. `shadow` means the decision was actually evaluated and no execution was affected by the result, whether or not a run enclosed it. `applied` means the route governed a real execution. Route readiness counts `applied` and nothing else: an advisory or shadow observation is real evidence of routing behaviour and never evidence that a route was applied. Optional, so observations predating this field stay valid; absent means the mode was not recorded, not that it was advisory or shadow, and an absent value is never counted as applied. An `applied` observation must carry `execution_run_id`; that invariant is enforced by the emitter and its tests rather than by schema conditionals.

grounding.description: How much of the candidate's evidence was verbatim. Optional: records predating this field carry no grounding, and its absence means unmeasured, never zero. Present so a FAIL can distinguish an invented citation from one paraphrased item out of five.

escalation_reason.description: Why the route escalated. `context-window-exceeded` and `context-truncated` both mean the model was not given the material the verifier checks against, and they differ by when that was discovered: `context-window-exceeded` is a refusal before inference, when the prompt does not fit the configured window; `context-truncated` is discovered afterwards, when the backend reports having processed fewer prompt tokens than were sent. Neither is `model-unavailable` — the model was reachable and willing; the material was not. Both must stay distinguishable from `verification-failed`, which means the model saw the material and cited it wrongly. `generation-timeout` is the caller's deadline expiring while the backend was generating: it was reached, it accepted the request and it was producing tokens, so nothing about it was unavailable. The rule is where the run stopped, not how long it took — backend reached and generation started and deadline exceeded is `generation-timeout`; a backend that cannot be reached or a model that cannot be invoked is `model-unavailable`. Keeping them apart matters because a store of timeouts recorded as `model-unavailable` claims an unreachable-runtime path was exercised when it never was.
